documentation.summary: AI labs and independent researchers use a multi-layered approach to blind evaluation of AI-generated code. The core pattern is: define tasks without exposing them to the model during training (contamination resistance), run evaluation in isolated harnesses (Harbor/SWE-bench), grade deterministically where possible (unit tests pass/fail), and use independent or cross-lab reviewers for subjective quality. Key frameworks include Anthropic Bloom, OpenAI Evals, SWE-bench Verified, Terminal-Bench 2.0, LiveCodeBench, and cybersecurity suites (CyberSecEval, CAIBench).

common_patterns.pattern: Tasks authored independently of the model under test
common_patterns.when_to_use: Always — the strongest blind evals source tasks from parties with no stake in the model being tested
common_patterns.example: SWE-bench: GitHub issues written by real users. BIG-Bench: tasks by external researchers. LiveCodeBench: competitive programming problems from independent platforms.

common_patterns.when_to_use: Whenever the task has an objectively correct answer (code correctness, bug fixes, security checks)
common_patterns.example: SWE-bench Verified: solution must fix failing tests without breaking passing tests. HumanEval: 164 Python tasks graded by unit tests. CyberSecEval: pass/fail by security static analysis tools.
Terminal-Bench: 5-15 samples per task across staggered batches. Bloom: 100 rollouts repeated 3 times. Report pass@k alongside mean scores.

common_patterns.pattern: Rolling benchmark updates for contamination resistance
common_patterns.when_to_use: Long-lived benchmarks that risk training set leakage over time
common_patterns.example: LiveCodeBench adds new competitive programming problems monthly — models cannot be trained on the test set. AntiLeakBench constructs samples with knowledge provably absent from training sets.

common_patterns.when_to_use: Publishing official benchmark results for frontier model releases
common_patterns.example: Terminal-Bench 2.0 reports both original lab scores and Anthropic's independent reproduction. The Anthropic-OpenAI joint eval exercise (June-July 2025) ran Anthropic's internal alignment evals against OpenAI models.

common_patterns.pattern: Blinded human evaluation for subjective tasks
common_patterns.when_to_use: Open-ended tasks where code correctness alone does not capture quality (style, maintainability, design)
common_patterns.example: OpenAI and Anthropic use randomized blinded tests where human evaluators or external labeling agencies judge outputs without knowing which model produced them.

common_patterns.pattern: Auto-generated scenarios (not hand-crafted) for behavioral evals
common_patterns.when_to_use: Evaluating model tendencies/behaviors rather than task completion
common_patterns.example: Anthropic Bloom: 4-stage pipeline (Understanding -> Ideation -> Rollout -> Judgment) generates diverse scenarios from a researcher-specified behavior. Prevents unconscious bias from scenario authors.

common_patterns.when_to_use: Agentic coding tasks requiring tool use or multi-step execution
common_patterns.example: Harbor runs Terminal-Bench 2.0 in fresh containers per task. SWE-bench uses Docker containers per repository. Prevents state leakage between tasks.

common_patterns.when_to_use: Complex coding tasks with multiple correctness dimensions
common_patterns.example: SWE-bench: (1) Does code run? (2) Do failing tests now pass? (3) Are existing passing tests unbroken? All three gates must pass.

common_patterns.when_to_use: Safety and security evaluations seeking failure modes rather than average-case performance
common_patterns.example: OpenAI external red team network. Japan AISI Red Teaming Guide v1.10 (March 2025). Humane Intelligence Asia-Pacific multilingual exercise. Red teamers probe the black-box API without seeing internal alignment methods.

gotchas.solution: Do not use HumanEval as a primary benchmark in 2025+. Frontier models score 93%+. Contamination is well-documented. Use SWE-bench Verified, LiveCodeBench, or BigCodeBench instead.
gotchas.example: A model scoring 95% on HumanEval reveals nothing about its ability to fix real bugs in production codebases.

gotchas.issue: Lab-published scores diverging from independent real-world results
gotchas.solution: Always require independent reproduction. Lab scores often rely on complex, high-compute prompting not representative of developer out-of-the-box experience.
gotchas.example: Terminal-Bench 2.0 reports both the original lab's score and Anthropic's independent re-run on the same harness.

gotchas.solution: Use model grading only for tasks without deterministic answers. Always pair with at least one other grading method. Avoid using the same model family to grade its own outputs.
gotchas.example: Anthropic uses Claude as grader for open-ended tasks but supplements with code-based and human grading for high-stakes assessments.

gotchas.solution: Limit to 2-3 benchmarks per release. Rotate benchmark versions. Monitor for suspiciously rapid improvement on a single benchmark. Maintain strictly held-out test sets never touched during development.
gotchas.example: SWE-bench Verified is resistant: fixing real GitHub bugs requires general coding ability, not benchmark-specific tricks.

gotchas.issue: In-house red teaming is insufficiently blind
gotchas.solution: Use external red team networks or independent third parties. Diverse evaluators who don't share the model developers' harm classifications and cultural assumptions.
gotchas.example: OpenAI requires third-party evaluators to independently confirm safety claims. CISA documents TEVV methodology for independent AI evaluation.

gotchas.issue: Single-run scores are statistically meaningless for stochastic models
gotchas.solution: Run 5-15 samples per task minimum. Use staggered batches. Report confidence intervals. Use pass@k metric.
gotchas.example: Terminal-Bench 2.0: 5-15 samples per task with 1x guaranteed / 3x ceiling resource allocation.

examples.title: Anthropic Bloom: 4-Stage Behavioral Evaluation Pipeline
examples.description: Bloom generates behavioral evaluations without hand-crafting scenarios, reducing evaluator bias.
examples.code:
# Stage 1: Understanding
# Researcher specifies behavior: e.g., 'self-preferential bias'
# Bloom parses the trait into measurable dimensions

# Stage 2: Ideation
# Bloom auto-generates diverse scenarios where the behavior could manifest
# (NOT written by the researcher or the model team)

# Stage 3: Rollout
# Each scenario is run against the model via LiteLLM
# Supports any frontier model: Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, etc.
# 100 rollouts per behavior, repeated 3 times for statistical validity

# Stage 4: Judgment
# Independent judge (model or human) scores each rollout
# Outputs: frequency rate + severity distribution
# Results exported as Inspect-compatible transcripts for third-party verification

# Key blind-testing property:
# Scenarios are generated FRESH per evaluation run
# The model team does not write the test cases
# Any lab can re-run using the same pipeline on their own models
examples.output: Behavioral quantification: frequency=12%, severity_mean=0.43 across 300 rollouts of 'self-preferential bias' on 16 frontier models

examples.title: SWE-bench Verified: Staged Deterministic Grading
examples.description: Uses pre-existing, externally-authored test suites from real repositories — the strongest structural blind eval design.
examples.code:
# Task sourcing (blind by design):
# 1. Real GitHub issues reported by actual users
# 2. Issues post-training-cutoff — model cannot have memorized the fix
# 3. Repository has existing test suite written by the repo's own maintainers

# Evaluation harness:
# 1. Give model the GitHub issue text + repository code
# 2. Model generates a code patch
# 3. Apply patch to repository in isolated Docker container
# 4. Run repository's test suite

# Grading gates (all deterministic, no human preference):
# Gate 1: Does the patched code run without errors?
# Gate 2: Do the failing tests now pass? (issue is fixed)
# Gate 3: Do all previously-passing tests still pass? (no regression)
# PASS = all three gates pass

# Why it resists contamination:
# Real-world tasks require understanding the specific codebase
# Cannot be solved by memorizing patterns from a benchmark dataset
# Test suite is authored by the repo maintainers, NOT the evaluators
examples.output: Score: 80%+ for top agentic systems in 2025 (vs 1.96% baseline in 2024)

examples.title: Cross-Lab Blind Eval: Anthropic x OpenAI Joint Exercise (2025)
examples.description: Each lab evaluates the other's models using their own eval framework — true structural independence.
examples.code:
# June-July 2025 exercise:
# 1. Anthropic selects its strongest internal alignment evaluations
# 2. Anthropic runs those evals against OpenAI's leading public models
#    via API access (black box — no training data or internals exposed)
# 3. OpenAI does not control the evaluation harness or grading criteria
# 4. Results are compared against OpenAI's own internal safety assessments
# 5. Disagreements are documented and published

# Blind properties:
# - Evaluators (Anthropic) have no stake in the model (OpenAI's)
# - Model team (OpenAI) does not control the test design
# - Black-box API access only — no internals exposed
# - Results published regardless of which lab's model performs better

integration_points.usage: Reference for designing independent test suites in the chunk-coder TDD workflow and plan-architect test architecture
integration_points.notes: Key takeaways: use deterministic grading, source tasks externally, run multiple samples, and keep test sets strictly held out
